findings.title: An upstream purchase-verification failure was reported as the business denial RTG-11001 (403) instead of a dependency failure
findings.business_risk: A rating submission returned 403 Only verified purchasers can rate this product while the upstream call had failed with a socket read timeout. A failure to determine was indistinguishable from a real denial.
findings.technical_risk: The catch swallowed the transport fault and returned false, so the orderService circuit breaker never recorded the failure and never opened.
findings.current_implementation: catch RestClientException returns false; the caller maps false to ErrorCode.RATING_NOT_ELIGIBLE.
findings.target_implementation: The upstream failure escapes the guarded call as BusinessException.serviceUnavailable (503 ERR-0503) with the cause preserved; the circuit breaker records it; a fallback maps an open breaker to the same dependency failure; a genuine not-eligible answer still returns 403 RTG-11001.
acceptance_criteria: An upstream transport failure on the eligibility check yields 503 with code ERR-0503 and never 403 with code RTG-11001
A genuine eligible=false answer from order-service still yields 403 with code RTG-11001
A missing or malformed payload from order-service is a dependency failure, not a denial
The circuit breaker that guards the call observes the upstream failure
findings.notes: Rule R19 was added to docs/PATTERNS.md for this class of defect.

findings.title: Five duplicated ServiceTokenProvider classes fetched the Keycloak token over a non-pooled connection with no Accept header, no retry and, in search-service, no timeout at all
findings.business_risk: Under load the token fetch stalled, every concurrent caller serialised behind the refresh lock, and the rating request took 33.9 s before failing.
findings.technical_risk: SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory opens a new connection per call with no pooling, the read timeout was 5 s, and search-service set no timeout at all.
findings.current_implementation: Five near-identical provider classes, one per service, each with its own request factory.
findings.target_implementation: One shared KeycloakServiceTokenProvider in common-keycloak with a pooled HttpClient, an Accept: application/json default header, a bounded retry inside a total refresh budget, automatic transport retries disabled so the policy is in one place, and a failure cooldown that collapses a refresh herd. The five service classes became thin adapters.
acceptance_criteria: The Keycloak token fetch uses a pooled HTTP client with a bounded connect and read timeout
The token request sends Accept: application/json
A transient failure is retried within a total refresh budget and a persistent failure raises a typed exception
A failure is not re-attempted by the next caller inside the cooldown window
The five service providers no longer duplicate the token logic
findings.notes: The test drives a real JDK HTTP server, so it exercises the wire behaviour rather than a mock.

findings.title: One Keycloak admin-client property served two different OAuth clients, so the application-realm service account could never authenticate
findings.business_risk: auth-service failed to start with HttpClientErrorException$Unauthorized from getServiceAccountAccessToken, so the platform could not issue tokens.
findings.technical_risk: shop.keycloak.admin-client-id (default admin-cli) was used for the master-realm password grant and for the application-realm client_credentials grant, but admin-cli exists only in the master realm.
findings.current_implementation: The client_credentials grant sent client_id=admin-cli against the ecommerce realm.
findings.target_implementation: A distinct service-account-client-id property (default ecommerce-admin) drives the client_credentials grant, while the master-realm password grant keeps admin-cli.
acceptance_criteria: The client_credentials grant sends the configured service account client id
The master-realm password grant keeps the master-realm admin client id

findings.title: The carrier call happened before the idempotency guard, so two duplicate CONFIRMED events created two parcels
findings.business_risk: A duplicate order event produced two physical parcels with one shipment row and one tracking number.
findings.technical_risk: The guard was a read that the carrier call invalidated, and the unique index fired only after the side effect.
findings.current_implementation: existsByOrderId was checked, then the carrier was called, then the row was inserted.
findings.target_implementation: The order id is claimed in a shipment_creation_tasks row before the carrier call; a partial unique index on order_id arbitrates the claim; the carrier request carries a deterministic Idempotency-Key.
acceptance_criteria: Three duplicate CONFIRMED events for one order produce exactly one shipment row, one creation task and one carrier call

findings.title: A carrier client exception was thrown away, so a failed shipment creation was lost
findings.business_risk: A carrier outage silently dropped the shipment and the order event dead-lettered.
findings.technical_risk: The exception escaped the consumer and nothing recorded that a parcel had to be created.
findings.current_implementation: The carrier exception propagated out of the consumer.
findings.target_implementation: The failure is recorded on the creation task with an attempt count and a next attempt time, and a retry worker picks it up.
acceptance_criteria: A carrier failure is recorded on the creation task and rescheduled instead of being lost

findings.title: The carrier client declared no HTTP timeout
findings.business_risk: A stalled carrier held the consumer thread and the parcel creation forever.
findings.technical_risk: The request factory had no connect or read timeout.
findings.current_implementation: The carrier RestClient used the default JDK request factory with no timeout.
findings.target_implementation: The carrier request factory declares a connect and read timeout inside a budget.
acceptance_criteria: A stalled carrier is abandoned inside the declared timeout budget

findings.title: changelog-003-webhook-retry violated a CHECK constraint, which blocked changesets 004, 005 and 006 from applying
findings.business_risk: The shipping schema could not be migrated past changeset 003, so the webhook retry feature could not be deployed.
findings.technical_risk: The 003 backfill writes status FAILED_RETRYABLE while the CHECK created in 001 allowed only PROCESSED and FAILED.
findings.target_implementation: A new changeset 002b widens the constraint before 003 runs; the already applied changesets 001 to 006 are untouched so their checksums stay valid.
acceptance_criteria: The whole changelog chain applies to an empty database
The whole chain applies to a database that already holds FAILED webhook event rows

findings.title: The reconciliation path bypassed the shipment finite state machine
findings.business_risk: The sweeper could move a shipment into a state the business does not allow.
findings.technical_risk: The status field had a public setter, so any caller could write an illegal transition.
findings.current_implementation: The reconciliation sweep assigned the status directly.
findings.target_implementation: The state machine owns every transition, the status setters are closed, and the sweep goes through the state machine with a per-row error boundary.
acceptance_criteria: A shipment the state machine forbids to auto-deliver is left untouched by the reconciliation sweep
No public setter can write the shipment status

findings.title: A late webhook could resurrect a DELIVERY_FAILED shipment
findings.business_risk: A shipment that had already failed delivery was moved back into transit by a late carrier callback.
findings.technical_risk: The state machine allowed the DELIVERY_FAILED to IN_TRANSIT edge.
findings.current_implementation: The DELIVERY_FAILED to IN_TRANSIT edge existed in the state machine.
findings.target_implementation: The edge is removed; an operator retry is the only way out of DELIVERY_FAILED; the webhook path uses the state machine.
acceptance_criteria: A late webhook cannot resurrect a DELIVERY_FAILED shipment

findings.title: Webhook retry rows had no claim, so several instances processed the same retry
findings.business_risk: The same carrier webhook was retried several times in parallel.
findings.technical_risk: The scheduler selected due rows without locking them.
findings.current_implementation: Due rows were read and processed without an exclusive claim.
findings.target_implementation: A conditional update claims the row with a claimed_at stamp and the claim is released on failure.
acceptance_criteria: A webhook retry row is claimed exclusively by one instance

findings.title: The outbox relay selected its head row with MIN(id), so a locked head row blocked every other row
findings.business_risk: One stuck row stopped the whole shipping outbox from draining.
findings.technical_risk: The claim selected MIN(id) and then locked it, so the head of line blocked the relay.
findings.current_implementation: The claim took the minimum id and locked it.
findings.target_implementation: The claim selects with ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so a locked row is skipped.
acceptance_criteria: A locked head row does not block the next pending row

findings.title: The reconciliation query had no matching index
findings.business_risk: The webhook retry scan degraded as the table grew.
findings.technical_risk: The status and next retry columns were not indexed.
findings.current_implementation: No index supported the due-retry scan.
findings.target_implementation: The index matches the due-retry predicate.
acceptance_criteria: The index exists in the migrated database

findings.title: The soft-delete restriction did not match the partial index, so a soft-deleted shipment still occupied the live key
findings.business_risk: A soft-deleted shipment still blocked the creation of a new shipment for the same order.
findings.technical_risk: The query restriction and the partial index disagreed on the deleted predicate.
findings.current_implementation: The soft-deleted rows were visible to the query path.
findings.target_implementation: The restriction matches the partial index and the creation claim reopens the soft-deleted row.
acceptance_criteria: A soft-deleted shipment is invisible and does not block a new one

findings.title: Shipment events had no foreign key to their shipment
findings.business_risk: An event could point at a shipment that does not exist.
findings.technical_risk: The relation was not enforced by the database.
findings.target_implementation: The foreign key is added, validated for existing rows and enforced for new rows.
acceptance_criteria: The foreign key exists in the migrated database

findings.title: A null provider event id was swallowed instead of rejected
findings.business_risk: Two carrier callbacks without an event id were indistinguishable.
findings.technical_risk: The missing id was absorbed and the insert violation was not classified by constraint.
findings.current_implementation: The missing event id was logged and processing continued.
findings.target_implementation: A signed payload without an event id is rejected with a bad request before any write, and an insert violation is classified by constraint name.
acceptance_criteria: A signed payload without an event id is rejected with a bad request
A constraint violation that is not the carrier event index is rejected with a bad request

findings.title: Permanently failed outbox rows were never surfaced
findings.business_risk: An event that could never be published disappeared without any signal.
findings.technical_risk: The relay exhausted its retries and left the row in a retry state forever.
findings.current_implementation: The exhausted row stayed in FAILED_RETRYABLE and was not counted.
findings.target_implementation: The exhausted row is parked as DEAD, counted by a metric, and purged by the retention scheduler.
acceptance_criteria: An event whose retries are exhausted is parked as dead and counted
The retention scheduler purges the dead rows
